entries.question: How do taxes work?
entries.answer: Taxes are money you pay to the government from your income. Your employer automatically deducts taxes from your paycheck. Every April 15th you file a tax return. If you overpaid you get a refund.

entries.question: What is a tax refund?
entries.answer: A tax refund is money the government owes you back when you paid more taxes than you owed. File your taxes at IRS.gov for free and get your refund in about 21 days.

entries.question: What is a credit score?
entries.answer: A credit score is a number from 300 to 850. Above 700 is good. Above 800 is excellent. Banks use it to decide if they give you loans or credit cards. Build it by paying bills on time every month.

entries.question: How do I build credit from zero?
entries.answer: Get a secured credit card by depositing $200-500. Use it for small purchases only. Pay the full balance every month. After 6-12 months you will have a real credit score.

entries.question: How do banks work?
entries.answer: Banks take money from savers and lend it to borrowers. They charge borrowers more interest than they pay savers — that difference is their profit. FDIC insures your money up to $250,000.

entries.question: How do I avoid bank fees?
entries.answer: Use online banks like Ally or Chime — they charge zero fees. If you use a traditional bank, maintain the minimum balance and only use your bank's ATMs to avoid fees.

entries.question: How does the US government work?
entries.answer: The US government has 3 branches. Congress makes laws. The President signs or vetoes them. The Supreme Court makes sure laws follow the Constitution. This prevents any one person from getting too much power.

entries.question: How do I vote in the US?
entries.answer: To vote you must be a US citizen, at least 18, and registered. In California register at registertovote.ca.gov. Local elections matter most — they are often decided by just a few hundred votes.

entries.question: How do I start a business?
entries.answer: Pick a name, register an LLC with your state (costs $70 in California), get a free EIN from IRS.gov, open a business bank account. An LLC protects your personal money if the business gets sued.

entries.question: What are my rights if police stop me?
entries.answer: Stay calm and keep hands visible. Say 'I am invoking my right to remain silent.' Ask 'Am I free to go?' Do not consent to a search. If arrested say 'I want a lawyer' and stop talking.

entries.question: What are my rights as a tenant?
entries.answer: In California your landlord must give 24 hours notice before entering. They must return your security deposit within 21 days of moving out. Document everything with photos when you move in.

entries.question: How do I start investing?
entries.answer: Open a Roth IRA at Fidelity or Vanguard for free. Buy an S&P 500 index fund like VOO. Invest small amounts regularly. Time is your biggest advantage — start as early as possible.

entries.question: Why is my paycheck less than my salary?
entries.answer: Federal and state taxes, Social Security (6.2%), and Medicare (1.45%) are deducted automatically. In California you can lose 30-40% of your gross salary. Always negotiate your salary — employers expect it.

entries.question: How does health insurance work?
entries.answer: You pay a monthly premium. When you use healthcare you pay a deductible first, then insurance covers most costs. In the US one hospital visit without insurance can cost $30,000. Always have health insurance.

entries.question: How do I get financial aid for college?
entries.answer: Fill out the FAFSA form at studentaid.gov every year — it is free. You can get grants (free money), scholarships (merit-based), work-study jobs, or loans. Community college like GCC costs about $46 per unit.

entries.question: How does immigration work in the US?
entries.answer: A green card gives permanent residency. You can get one through family, employment, or asylum. After 5 years you can apply for citizenship. Always use official USCIS.gov — many scammers pose as immigration lawyers.

entries.question: What is a W-2 form?
entries.answer: A W-2 is a form your employer sends every January showing how much you earned and how much tax was withheld. You need it to file your taxes. Employers must send it by January 31st.

entries.question: What is compound interest?
entries.answer: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Online banks like Ally pay 4-5% on savings while traditional banks pay almost nothing. Start saving early — even small amounts grow significantly over time.

entries.question: What are my rights at work?
entries.answer: California minimum wage is $16/hour. Overtime over 8 hours per day must be paid at 1.5x your rate. You cannot be fired for discriminatory reasons. Report violations to the California Labor Commissioner.

entries.question: How do I take someone to small claims court?
entries.answer: Small claims court in California handles disputes up to $12,500 with no lawyer needed. It costs $30-75 to file. Legal Aid Foundation of LA provides free legal help for low-income people.

entries.question: How much is $1000 salary after taxes in California?
entries.answer: In California earning $1000 gross: Federal tax ~$120, Social Security ~$62, Medicare ~$14.50, California state tax ~$32. Total deductions ~$228. Your take-home pay is approximately $772. California has one of the highest state income taxes in the US.

entries.question: Which states have no income tax?
entries.answer: 9 states have no state income tax: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, and Wyoming. Living in these states means you keep more of your paycheck. However they often make up for it with higher sales tax or property tax.

entries.question: How much of my paycheck should I save?
entries.answer: The 50/30/20 rule is the most popular guideline. Spend 50% on needs (rent, food, utilities), 30% on wants (entertainment, dining out), and save 20%. If you earn $1000 take-home, save at least $200 every month. Even saving $50-100 a month is better than nothing — start small and increase over time.

entries.question: How much should I have in an emergency fund?
entries.answer: Financial experts recommend saving 3 to 6 months of living expenses in an emergency fund. If your monthly expenses are $2000, aim for $6000 to $12000. Keep it in a high-yield savings account at an online bank earning 4-5% interest. Never invest your emergency fund in stocks.

entries.question: What is a 401k and should I use it?
entries.answer: A 401k is a retirement savings account your employer offers. You contribute pre-tax money — meaning you pay less tax now. Many employers match your contributions up to 3-6% of your salary — that is free money. Always contribute at least enough to get the full employer match. The money grows tax-deferred until retirement.

entries.question: What is Social Security and why is it taken from my paycheck?
entries.answer: Social Security is a government program that provides income when you retire, become disabled, or die leaving dependents. 6.2% of your paycheck goes to Social Security automatically. Your employer also pays 6.2% on your behalf. You can start collecting Social Security benefits at age 62, but waiting until 67 or 70 gives you larger monthly payments.

entries.question: What is Medicare and why is it taken from my paycheck?
entries.answer: Medicare is government health insurance for people 65 and older. 1.45% of every paycheck goes to Medicare tax. Your employer also pays 1.45%. You become eligible for Medicare at age 65. Medicaid is different — it is health insurance for low-income people of any age.

entries.question: How do I pay off credit card debt?
entries.answer: Two popular methods: Avalanche method — pay minimum on all cards and put extra money toward the card with highest interest rate. Saves the most money. Snowball method — pay off smallest balance first for quick wins and motivation. Never pay only the minimum — at 20% interest, $1000 debt takes 5+ years to pay off making minimums only.

entries.question: Should I buy or lease a car?
entries.answer: Buying is better long-term — you own it and build equity. Leasing has lower monthly payments but you never own it and have mileage limits. For a car loan, aim for a term of 48-60 months maximum. Never finance a car for 72-84 months — you end up paying far more than the car is worth. Put at least 20% down if possible.

entries.question: How do I buy a house?
entries.answer: Save at least a 20% down payment to avoid PMI (private mortgage insurance). Get pre-approved for a mortgage before shopping. Your monthly payment should not exceed 28% of your gross income. In Los Angeles the median home price is over $800,000 — you would need $160,000 down. Check first-time homebuyer programs in California for assistance.

entries.question: How do taxes work if I am self-employed or freelance?
entries.answer: As a freelancer you receive a 1099 form instead of a W-2. You must pay self-employment tax of 15.3% (Social Security + Medicare) on top of regular income tax. Pay quarterly estimated taxes in April, June, September, and January to avoid penalties. Track all business expenses — they are tax deductible. Consider forming an LLC to protect yourself.

keywords: what do i need bank account
entries.question: What do I need to open a bank account?
entries.answer: To open a bank account you need a government-issued photo ID (driver's license, passport, or state ID), your Social Security Number or ITIN, and sometimes an initial deposit. Online banks like Chime and Ally require no minimum deposit and charge zero fees. If you have no SSN, some banks accept an ITIN (Individual Taxpayer Identification Number).

entries.question: What is a good credit score?
entries.answer: Credit scores range from 300 to 850. Poor: 300-579. Fair: 580-669. Good: 670-739. Very Good: 740-799. Exceptional: 800-850. With a score above 740 you qualify for the best interest rates on loans and credit cards. Above 800 and you are in the top tier — lenders compete for your business.

entries.question: How long does it take to build a good credit score?
entries.answer: Starting from zero you can have a credit score within 3-6 months of opening your first credit account. Building a good score of 700+ typically takes 1-2 years of on-time payments. Building an excellent score of 800+ usually takes 5-7 years of responsible credit use. Negative items like missed payments stay on your report for 7 years.

entries.question: How do I dispute an error on my credit report?
entries.answer: Get your free credit report at AnnualCreditReport.com (the only official free site). If you find an error, dispute it directly with the credit bureau (Equifax, Experian, or TransUnion) at their website. They must investigate within 30 days. If the error is confirmed, they must remove it. Disputing correct negative information will not help — only actual errors can be removed.

entries.question: What are the taxes like living in Glendale California?
entries.answer: Glendale is in Los Angeles County, California. You pay: Federal income tax, California state income tax (among the highest in the US), and no additional Glendale city income tax. On $1000 gross you take home approximately $772. California sales tax in Glendale is 10.25%. Property tax is about 1.1% of assessed value per year.

entries.question: How much is $1000 salary after taxes in Los Angeles?
entries.answer: In Los Angeles earning $1000 gross: Federal tax ~$120, Social Security ~$62, Medicare ~$14.50, California state tax ~$32, SDI (State Disability Insurance) ~$9. Total deductions ~$237. Your take-home pay is approximately $763. LA has no additional city income tax unlike New York City.

entries.question: What is the minimum wage in California?
entries.answer: California minimum wage is $16.50 per hour as of 2025 — one of the highest in the US. Fast food workers have a higher minimum of $20/hour. Some cities like San Francisco have even higher minimums. At $16.50/hour working 40 hours a week you earn $660 before taxes, approximately $550-580 take-home.

entries.question: Can I work and pay taxes without a Social Security Number?
entries.answer: Yes. You can apply for an ITIN (Individual Taxpayer Identification Number) from the IRS. An ITIN lets you file taxes and open bank accounts but does not authorize work or provide Social Security benefits. To get an ITIN fill out Form W-7 at IRS.gov. Many immigrants use ITINs to build credit and financial history in the US.

keywords: how much should i pay rent
entries.question: How much should I spend on rent?
entries.answer: The 30% rule says spend no more than 30% of your gross income on rent. If you earn $3000/month gross, keep rent at $900 or less. In Los Angeles and Glendale average rent is $2000-2500 for a 1-bedroom, which is very high relative to incomes. Consider roommates, living further from downtown, or looking in Burbank, Pasadena, or San Bernardino for lower rents.

entries.question: What is a W-4 form?
entries.answer: A W-4 is a form you fill out when starting a new job telling your employer how much tax to withhold from your paycheck. If you claim too many allowances, too little is withheld and you owe taxes in April. If you claim too few, too much is withheld and you get a refund. For most single people with one job, following the standard W-4 instructions works fine.

entries.question: What is a 529 plan?
entries.answer: A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged savings account specifically for education expenses. Your money grows tax-free and withdrawals for qualified education expenses (tuition, books, room and board) are also tax-free. Many states offer additional tax deductions for contributions. You can use it for college, vocational school, or even K-12 private school tuition up to $10,000 per year.

entries.question: What is inflation and how does it affect me?
entries.answer: Inflation means prices increase over time so your money buys less. The US Federal Reserve targets 2% annual inflation. When inflation is high (like 8% in 2022) your savings lose value fast. To beat inflation your money needs to grow faster than the inflation rate. Savings accounts at 4-5% currently beat inflation. Keeping cash under a mattress is the worst option — it loses value every year.

entries.question: What is the Federal Reserve and why does it matter?
entries.answer: The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is the US central bank. It controls interest rates to manage inflation and unemployment. When inflation is high the Fed raises rates making borrowing more expensive — this slows the economy. When the economy is slow the Fed lowers rates making borrowing cheaper to stimulate growth. Fed rate decisions affect your mortgage, car loan, credit card rates, and savings account interest.

entries.question: How does eviction work in California?
entries.answer: In California a landlord must give written notice before evicting: 3 days for non-payment of rent, 30 days for month-to-month tenants (60 days if you lived there 1+ year). The landlord must then file in court if you do not leave. You have the right to fight the eviction in court. The entire process takes 1-3 months minimum. Document everything and contact a tenant rights organization if threatened with eviction.

entries.question: What are the rights and benefits of DACA?
entries.answer: DACA (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) allows eligible undocumented immigrants who came to the US as children to receive a 2-year renewable work permit and protection from deportation. DACA recipients can get a Social Security Number, driver's license, and work legally. DACA does not provide a path to citizenship. Renew your DACA before it expires — do not wait until the last minute. Use official USCIS.gov only.

entries.question: How much does it cost to start an LLC in California?
entries.answer: In California an LLC costs: $70 filing fee to the Secretary of State, plus $800 annual franchise tax (minimum, due every year even if you make no money), plus $20 for a Statement of Information due within 90 days of forming. Total first year cost approximately $890. After that the $800 annual tax continues every year. Use bizfile.sos.ca.gov to file online.

entries.question: How do I get an EIN number for my business?
entries.answer: An EIN (Employer Identification Number) is your business tax ID from the IRS. It is completely free at IRS.gov/ein. The online application takes about 10 minutes and you get your EIN immediately. You need it to open a business bank account, hire employees, and file business taxes. Never pay anyone to get you an EIN — it is always free directly from the IRS.

entries.question: How do student loans work?
entries.answer: Federal student loans have fixed interest rates and flexible repayment options. Income-Driven Repayment (IDR) plans cap your payments at 5-10% of your discretionary income. Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) forgives remaining debt after 10 years if you work for government or non-profits. Never miss payments — it destroys your credit. Always choose federal loans over private loans which have fewer protections.

entries.question: How do I check my credit score for free?
entries.answer: You can check your credit score free in several ways: Credit Karma (free, shows TransUnion and Equifax scores), your bank or credit card app (many show your score for free), AnnualCreditReport.com (free full credit reports from all 3 bureaus). Never pay for your credit score. Checking your own score does NOT hurt your credit — only hard inquiries from applications affect it.

entries.question: What is APR?
entries.answer: APR stands for Annual Percentage Rate. It is the true yearly cost of borrowing money including fees and interest. A credit card with 20% APR charges about 1.67% per month on your balance. A mortgage with 7% APR means you pay 7% per year on the remaining balance. Always compare APR not just the interest rate when comparing loans — the APR includes all costs.

entries.question: What does tax deductible mean?
entries.answer: Tax deductible means an expense reduces your taxable income. If you earn $50,000 and have $5,000 in deductions, you only pay tax on $45,000. Common deductions: student loan interest, home mortgage interest, charitable donations, business expenses. Self-employed people can deduct home office, car mileage, phone, and equipment used for work. Keep receipts for everything you plan to deduct.
